title: How Elementary Schools Keep Men Out Of College
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: Wexler takes the record gender gap in college enrollment and argues its root may lie in early literacy instruction rather than in single-sex schooling or male role models. She grants that weak phonics teaching and mismatched expectations, as argued by Whitmire and Petrilli, play a part, but says the typical elementary day is also built around independent work and skills-based comprehension practice that bores boys and invites discipline problems. Drawing on her classroom observations, she contrasts skills-and-worksheets classrooms with a second-grade class using a content-rich curriculum with knowledge-building read-alouds, where discussion was rich and disciplinary incidents were few. She admits the evidence is anecdotal but points to a study showing a science-centered kindergarten curriculum boosted reading motivation for all children and comprehension more for boys. The bucket is Learning & Curriculum because her argument is about how literacy curriculum is designed, not about masculinity.
points: Wexler locates part of the male college gap in early literacy instruction, not only in phonics gaps or teacher expectations.
Independent work and decontextualized comprehension skills like finding the main idea are boring and push young boys toward disruption.
Her classroom observations show a content-rich curriculum with read-alouds and discussion producing engagement and few disciplinary incidents, even with many boys.
A kindergarten science-content curriculum raised reading motivation for all and comprehension more for boys, though she says more research is needed.
quotes: Women increasingly outnumber men on college campuses, with devastating implications for the life chances of American males. The root of the problem may lie in our misguided approach to early reading instruction.

The typical elementary school day looks as though it was designed to entice boys into committing disciplinary infractions. During the bulk of instructional time, the teacher works directly with a series of small groups while the rest of the class is supposedly engaged in independent work.

Much of the reading block is devoted to comprehension practice that foregrounds “skills” like “finding the main idea,” with students independently reading simple books on random topics. Or kids may be given worksheets or computer programs that ask them to do things like compare fruits and vegetables, on the baseless theory that mastering the “skill” of comparing and contrasting will equip them to read complex text.

Unfortunately for the teacher, it had 14 boys and six girls, and most of the time it was a scene of barely controlled chaos. One day a tiny girl, encouraged by the teacher, pleaded for quiet, explaining that she couldn’t think with all the noise.
But after the story explained that urine was actually cleaner than saliva, it was Amir—to the teacher’s surprise—who asked thoughtfully if that meant people could drink their own urine.

But a recent study found that a kindergarten curriculum centered on science content significantly boosted reading motivation for both boys and girls—and its positive impact on reading comprehension was greater for boys. We need more research on the effects of content-rich elementary curricula, especially as they relate to boys and literacy.
But it could prevent untold numbers of boys from concluding that school just isn’t for them at a time when their academic careers have barely started.
